 Liberty students cast ballots in 2026 Virginia elections
 November 17, 2026 | Arianna Hooker
 News
 Share to Socials
 Liberty University students lined the halls to vote on Election Day, Nov. 3 in the Montview Alumni Ballroom for the 2026 Virginia General and Special Elections. 
 Voting began at 6 a.m. and concluded at 7 p.m.  
 Students voted for members of the United States House of Representatives and Senate, Lynchburg City Council and on three proposed amendments to the Virginia Constitution.  
 Liberty University Student Body Vice President Josie Huyard explained the significance of voting. 
 “Voting is so important because it’s our way that we can voice our concerns in government,” Huyard said. 
 Huyard emphasized how the ballot contained issues that affect everyone.   
 “It’s things that affect us every single day,” Huyard said. “It’s so important that we make sure that everyone votes.”  
 Democratic  incumbent  Sen. Mark Warner was elected to a fourth term in the Senate, according to the  Associated Press election results . 
 Democratic candidates Nat Marshall, Christina Delzingaro and Dave Henderson won the three Lynchburg City Council seats, according to  WDBJ7 election results . 
 All House seats on the ballot for Virginia were won by the Republican candidates, according to  WSET . 
 The three proposed state constitutional amendments about abortion, same-sex marriage and the automatic restoration of a felon’s political rights were passed. 
 The  first amendment  cemented  abortion as a constitutional right in Virginia . 
 Current Virginia law requires that three physicians sign off on an abortion after the second trimester. However, the passed amendment will require only one physician or abortion provider to sign off. 
 The passed amendment also contains vague wording stating every individual has the fundamental right to reproductive freedom, which endangers parental rights. 
 Sophomore Isaac Yarnell said abortion is an important issue for him.  
 “I think it’s the biggest moral crisis of any generation, ever,” Yarnell said. “Just look at the amount of lives that have been lost and the desensitization to human life.”  
 The second passed  amendment  will  enshrine same-sex marriage  into the state constitution will affirm “that two adults may marry regardless of sex, gender, or race.”  
 Students emphasized the importance on voting their biblical beliefs regarding marriage and life.  
 Sophomore Madelin Ousdahl shared how Christians should vote according to biblical values.  
 “I think it’s our duty as people living in a country that is claimed to be under God, to vote in such a manner that reflects biblical rights,” Ousdahl said. 
 The last passed  amendment  will  automatically restore all political rights , including the rights to vote, serve on a jury and carry a firearm, to felons upon release from incarceration. 
 Yarnell said Christians should become more involved.    
 “If you take the Christian aspects out of America, it ceases to become what America was meant to be,” Yarnell said. “Christians need to be more practical in how we’re going to defend for the future, because if we don’t vote, then godless people will.” 
 The amendments will go into  effect  January 1, 2027. 
 Hooker is a news reporter for The Liberty Champion.
